# Shift 22 Report - res_1 - Paper 1311.2485 "Continuous-time quantum error correction" (Oreshkov, 2013)

File: archive/quantum_error_correction/papers/1311.2485.txt (book chapter, Lidar & Brun eds.; line numbers below refer to this file).
Topic question: *Are surface codes with superconducting qubits capable of operating below fault-tolerant error thresholds?*

- Standard discrete QEC represents noise and correction as discrete CPTP maps with correction applied
after the noise; this is only an approximation, because a real correcting operation takes finite time and
under non-Markovian dynamics the effective map between corrections need not be CP at all (L42-49).
- **CTQEC**: noise *and* correction are continuous. Protected information sits in a subsystem HA of
HS = HA ⊗ HB ⊕ K; in the encoded basis for an [[n,1,r,d]] code, HS = HA ⊗(n-r-1 syndrome qubits)⊗(r gauge qubits)
(L15, L195-206). Multi-qubit QEC then reduces to protecting a *known* single-qubit state.
- **PZ quantum-jump / direct feedback**: ρ -> (1-κdt)ρ + κdt R(ρ), master equation
dρ/dt = L(ρ) + κJ(ρ), J(ρ) = R(ρ) - ρ (L60-73). Physical reading: coupling to a **stream of fresh

ancillas** that continuously pump out accumulated entropy, i.e. a cooling process; also implementable by
weak measurement + weak unitary (L103-108).
- **Weak map form**: ρ -> (1-ε²)ρ + ε²R(ρ) acting over a small but finite time τc, with effective
rate **κ = ε²/τc** (L96-101).
- **ADL indirect feedback**: stochastic master equation with continuous weak measurement of the stabilizer
generators Ml (Wiener-process jumps) plus correcting Hamiltonians Hr switched on with strength
λr(ρ) = λ sgn Tr([Πc, Hr]ρ), chosen to maximize instantaneous code-space fidelity (L128-154).
Weak X-measurement can be done with one ancilla: HX = -X ⊗ Y for time ~ε/2, then destructive ancilla
measurement, outcome probabilities p± = ½(1 ± ε Tr(Xρ)) (L584-600).
## 2. The "freezing" / Zeno argument

- Correctable error weight in a short step Δt is ∝ Δt, uncorrectable (higher-order) weight is O(Δt²);
therefore continuously applied correction stops accumulation, and in the limit Δt -> 0 the state
**freezes** (L112-119).
- Encoded-basis bound: ||dρA/dt|| ≤ B(1-α) + C√(α(1-α)), so keeping (1-α) small suppresses the
accumulation rate of uncorrectable errors; CTQEC is thus "the goal of keeping every syndrome qubit close
to |0>" (L340-364).
## 3. Weak measurement + feedback, and the honest limitation (quoted)

- "All these schemes are to a large extent **heuristic**, and their workings are not thoroughly
understood. The difficulty in rigorously motivating the construction of error-correction protocols based
on weak measurements and feedback is that stochastic evolutions are generally too complicated to study
analytically." (L155-162)
- Both schemes are related to known optimal single-qubit purification protocols: PZ ≈ fast average-fidelity
protocol (measure X, rotate about Y), ADL ≈ fastest-average-time protocol (measure Z, rotate about X);
optimality is claimed only w.r.t. these single-qubit criteria, not for their resource cost (L888-908).
- Retaining the measurement record would improve PZ only by O((1-α*_M)²) - i.e. PZ is "very close to

optimal" in the regime where 1-α*_M is small, but only if the relation between measurement strength and
correcting rotation (Eq. 36, L470-476) can be met (L910-925).
## 4. Numbers and performance (direct feedback, exactly solvable bit-flip models)

- Zeno bookkeeping: α(t) = 1 - Ct² + O(t³) (L1091), and balancing 2√C√(1-α)Δt against
κ(1-α)Δt gives 1 - α*_NM ≈ 4C/κ² vs 1 - α*_M ∝ 1/κ (L1414-1449); same 1/κ² conclusion argued
for general codes because each syndrome qubit in the encoded basis is Zeno-driven (L1450-1454).
- **Resource caveat**: ε ∝ g²τc², hence **κ ∝ g²τc** (L1462-1466). Shrinking τc to gain time
resolution lowers κ; the quadratic gain can outweigh the linear loss, giving a "seemingly paradoxical"
better performance at lower κ (L1468-1474). **This is the failure condition the director asked for.**
## 5. Answers to the four questions

**Q: Does continuous-time correction beat discrete-cycle correction, and under what conditions?**
The paper never benchmarks against a discrete-cycle protocol. What it shows is that CTQEC reaches perfect
protection in the limit of infinite correction rate (freezing), whereas a Markovian discrete cycle always
leaves O(1/r) residual uncorrectable weight that then produces logical errors at rate ~6γ/r (L1057-1077).
So the honest statement is: CTQEC's *floor* is lower and it avoids the dead time of a real correcting
operation, but there is no head-to-head comparison. CTQEC's advantage is real only if the weak operation is
genuinely continuous and cheap; the paper's own resource relation κ ∝ g²τc (L1466) says you pay for
faster resolution with lower correction rate.

**Q: Is the Zeno/freezing result a threshold result or something weaker?**
Much weaker, and it is *not* the foundation of the threshold theorem - the author says so explicitly. The
freezing argument is asymptotic and qualitative: correctable O(Δt) vs uncorrectable O(Δt²) (L112-119).
It has no code-size scaling, no logical error rate per cycle, no threshold constant, and no requirement
that errors be correctable in the discrete sense - it works even below the code's usual error radius
(indeed that is the point). It is also weaker in that it protects *quantum memory*: "So far, CTQEC has been
considered only as a method of protecting quantum memory. ... An important question in this respect is
whether CTQEC can be made fault tolerant" (L1503-1505). Fault tolerance assumes discrete transversal

operations; the author proposes looking for fault-tolerant implementations of a universal set of *weak*
operations, which is an open research programme. Treat the freezing/Zeno result as **an alternative
route to below-threshold behaviour, not a threshold theorem**.

**Q: What would a superconducting surface-code cycle have to look like to realize this?**
The paper contains no surface-code, superconducting, or hardware numbers at all; it is the director's
framing that a ~1 µs surface-code cycle is "coarse, not continuous". Within the paper's own framework
the requirements are explicit and demanding:
(i) τc ≪ the Zeno/bath correlation time, and γδt ≪ 1 ≪ κδt (L1405), i.e. weak, *fast*,
continuously repeated operations at a rate κ well above the noise rate;
(ii) a physically available weak syndrome measurement - the paper's own realization is an ancilla
coupled by HX = -X ⊗ Y, i.e. a two-qubit XX/YY-type interaction plus fast readout (L584-600);

(iii) enough control bandwidth to keep r = κ/λ large *and* linear in n (L1051-1055), since surface
codes have large n and many syndromes;
(iv) locality: the author flags scalability with 1-2 qubit Hamiltonians as an open problem (L1498-1502).
A 1 µs round with measurement/reset latencies of comparable size is in the regime where the
continuous-time description is a poor fit, and where the paper's freezing argument buys nothing beyond
what ordinary threshold analysis already gives.

**Q: What is irrelevant to surface codes, and why should the director not over-claim?**
- No surface code is mentioned anywhere; the only codes analysed are 1- and 3-qubit bit-flip codes
(L1218-1220, L1237-1238). No rotated/unrotated layout, no lattice, no decoder, no threshold value.
- Noise models are independent bit-flips (Markovian) or a single Ising-type bath spin H = γX⊗X
(L70, L1240-1250). No amplitude damping, no leakage, no measurement error, no crosstalk, no cosmic-ray
or quasi-static 1/f drift - the dominant superconducting failure modes. The weakly non-Markovian
bath is modeled as a *single* spin qubit, which is the most favourable possible limit.
- The ADL/feedback family is explicitly labelled heuristic (L155-162); the rigorous analysis exists only

for the quantum-jump (direct feedback) model (L19-23).
- CTQEC is memory protection only; fault tolerance is an open question raised by the author himself
(L1503-1505).
- So the defensible statement is: "continuous-time correction provides a Zeno/freezing mechanism and,
in non-Markovian noise, a 1/κ² rather than 1/κ residual-error law, which is a *complementary* argument
for suppressing logical errors; it is not evidence about surface codes or superconducting thresholds."
Any phrasing like "CTQEC shows surface codes can operate below threshold" would be an extrapolation the
paper does not support.

## Bottom line for the synthesis
Use 1311.2485 for definitional and conceptual framing only: it defines continuous-time correction, gives the
freezing mechanism, the Markovian 1/κ vs non-Markovian 1/κ² contrast, and the honest statement that
continuous-time protection is not yet fault tolerant. Let res_2/res_3/res_4 carry the surface-code and
superconducting evidence.

# Shift 24 Summary - res_1 - Paper 1311.2485 "Continuous-time quantum error correction" (Oreshkov, 2013)

## Paper type
Theory/review chapter (book chapter, Lidar & Brun eds.). No experiments, no superconducting hardware,
no numerical fault-tolerance thresholds. It provides the *framework* for thinking about continuous
error correction, not a surface-code threshold result.

## Core framework
- Discrete QEC formalism (CPTP noise map E + recovery R) idealizes both noise and correction as
instantaneous discrete maps. In reality correction takes finite time, and with non-Markovian noise the
system correlates with the environment, so effective maps between corrections need not even be CP.
- **CTQEC** = both noise and correction are continuous processes. Protected info lives in a *subsystem*
(subsystem principle); the author works in an "encoded basis" where HA = logical factor, plus
(n-r-1) syndrome qubit factors and r gauge qubits, for an [[n,1,r,d]] stabilizer code. This reduces
multi-qubit QEC to the single-qubit problem of protecting a *known* state.

- **Paz-Zurek (PZ) quantum-jump model / direct feedback**: instantaneous full correction operations
applied at random times with rate kappa. Master equation dρ/dt = L(ρ) + κJ(ρ), with jump generator
J(ρ) = R(ρ) - ρ. Physically: a stream of fresh ancillas weakly coupled and discarded, i.e. a
*cooling* process that continuously pumps out entropy.
- **ADL scheme / indirect feedback**: continuous weak syndrome (stabilizer) measurement + feedback
Hamiltonians whose strength λr(ρ) = λ sgn Tr([Πc, Hr]ρ) is chosen to maximize instantaneous
code-space fidelity. Weakened weak map: ρ -> (1-ε²)ρ + ε²R(ρ) over time τc, giving κ = ε²/τc.
Note in ADL, syndrome measurement is on the *code* stabilizers and correction acts back; in PZ the
role of X and Z measurements/rotations is swapped relative to the intuitive picture.

## Why continuous can beat discrete ("freezing")
Correctable error weight grows as O(Δt) per step while uncorrectable (higher-order) weight is O(Δt²).
So as correction becomes continuous, uncorrectable weight never accumulates: in the limit of infinite
correction rate the state *freezes*. The whole point is to suppress the second-order term.

## Performance results (direct feedback, bit-flip codes, exactly solvable models)
- Markovian, 3-qubit bit-flip code, ratio r = κ/λ: weight outside code space → 3/(4+r) ~ 1/r.
Encoded qubit then decays *inside* the code space like bare bit-flip noise at rate (6/r)γ, i.e.
overall decoherence reduced by ~r/6. In the limit r -> ∞ protection is perfect for all times.
- Uncorrected weight scales roughly **linearly with the number of qubits** for fixed κ, and the κ needed
to hold a given code-space overlap also scales ~linearly in n. Resource cost grows with code size.
- **Non-Markovian / Zeno regime (the headline result)**: for a system initially decoupled from its bath
the fidelity is α(t) = 1 - Ct² + O(t³). Balancing Zeno decay 2√C√(1-α)Δt against correction

κ(1-α)Δt gives quasi-stationary equilibrium fidelity
1 - α*_NM ≈ 4C/κ², vs 1 - α*_M ∝ 1/κ.
So effective error rate reduction improves **quadratically (κ²)** in the non-Markovian case but only
linearly (κ) in the Markovian case. Same 1/κ² scaling argued to hold for any code, since every
syndrome qubit in the encoded basis undergoes Zeno-type evolution.
- Valid only in the regime γδt << 1 << κδt, i.e. the weak correction must be *faster than the Zeno
time* to reveal the non-Markovian structure. Resource caveat: ε ∝ g²τc², so κ ∝ g²τc - shrinking
τc to raise time resolution lowers κ. The paper notes the "paradoxical" possibility that a *lower*

correction rate gives better performance because the quadratic κ² gain outweighs the linear loss.
- Error *prevention* (frequent syndrome measurement only, no correction) works only in the Zeno regime,
fails under Markovian assumptions, but allows lower redundancy (4-qubit encoding of 1 qubit vs 3-qubit
repetition for correction). Error correction therefore works in regimes where prevention fails, at the
cost of higher redundancy and added correcting unitaries.

## Relevance to the topic question (surface codes + superconducting qubits, below-threshold operation)
- CTQEC is an **alternative paradigm to discrete syndrome-extraction cycles**, not a threshold theorem.
It shifts the burden from "error rate per cycle < threshold" to "correction rate κ and time resolution
τc vs bath correlation time".
- Superconducting qubits plausibly sit in the favourable regime: long T1/T2 and quasi-static
(1/f, telegraph) noise mean bath memory is *not* negligible, i.e. evolution is non-Markovian at long
times - exactly where the Zeno/quadratic argument applies. This is the paper's strongest link to the
question, but it is a qualitative argument, not evidence.

- The paper contains **no** statement about surface codes specifically, no comparison of rotated vs
unrotated layouts, and no threshold numbers. Its examples are 1- and 3-qubit bit-flip codes.
- Direct/indirect feedback schemes are called "largely heuristic" and "not thoroughly understood" by the
author; the theoretical analysis is done only for the quantum-jump (direct feedback) model.
- Author's own open question, directly relevant to the review: "whether CTQEC can be made fault
tolerant" - FT theory assumes discrete transversal logical operations; he proposes looking for
fault-tolerant implementations of a universal set of *weak* operations. Also open: scalability with
local (1-2 qubit) Hamiltonians only, and whether an equilibrium-fidelity analogue exists for

## Key takeaways for the synthesis
1. CTQEC offers a second, independent route to below-threshold operation: continuous weak
measurement + feedback, where protection comes from a Zeno/freezing argument instead of a
threshold theorem. Nothing here contradicts threshold theory; it is a different resource assumption.
2. The single strongest quantitative claim: uncorrectable error weight 1/κ (Markovian) vs 1/κ²
(non-Markovian/Zeno) - super-linear returns on correction rate, conditional on resolving the Zeno
time scale.
3. Honest limitation: this paper is theory from 2013 with toy codes; any claim that "CTQEC enables
below-threshold surface codes on superconducting qubits" would be an extrapolation beyond the paper.

## Headline numbers for "can surface codes run below threshold on superconducting qubits?"

**Theoretical / benchmark thresholds**
- Matching-based decoders (MWPM and correlated variants) reach a *circuit-level* threshold of
roughly **0.5-1%** (2605.17156, Sec. 2.3).
- For the superconducting-inspired **SI1000** noise model the quoted surface-code threshold is

all land on **identical** logical error rates at every d and p tested (Table 4). Interpretation

offered by the authors: MWPM is already near-optimal *among factorized, independent-basis
decoders* in that regime.
- SMD's fitted scaling law uses the standard surface-code form p_L ~ (p/p_th)^floor((d+1)/2)
(also restated in 2504.19833).

**Superconducting error rates actually used in benchmarks (SI1000, relative to 2q gate rate p)**
| Operation | Rate |
|---|---|
| two-qubit CZ | p |
| single-qubit gate | p/10 |
| measurement readout | 5p |
| reset | 2p |
| idle (per round) | 4.2p |

Tested at p = 1e-3 to 1.5e-3, i.e. two-qubit error ~0.1-0.15%, readout ~0.5-0.75%.
Readout and idle dominate the budget - this is the structural reason the SI1000 threshold
(5e-3) sits far below the ideal 0.5-1%.

**Is the operating point below threshold? Yes on the benchmark, yes in hardware (secondhand).**
- 2605.17156 evaluates at p = 1.5e-3 with R = 120, "well below the SI1000 threshold p_th ~ 5e-3",
and reports monotonically falling per-cycle LER with d.
- On **Sycamore experimental data** (50k shots/round, four d=3 patches + one d=5 patch,
R = 1..25, X and Z memory): SMD ensemble reaches mean LER **2.94e-2 (d=3)** and
**3.00e-2 (d=5)**; dense Mamba (Lee et al.) 2.98e-2 / 3.03e-2; tensor-network near-MLD
3.05e-2 (d=3) and 2.98e-2 (d=5). So on the flagship superconducting dataset the neural
decoders are at or slightly past the tensor-network reference, and the experimental numbers

are *worse* than the synthetic SI1000 numbers by ~1.5 orders of magnitude - that gap is the
"theory vs experiment" gap in one line.
- The headline below-threshold demonstrations are cited but **not contained in this archive**:
Acharya et al., "QEC below the surface code threshold", Nature 2024 (Google, and a
superconducting processor with suppression factor lambda = 2.14 +/- 0.02 when increasing d);
Bluvstein et al. 2024 (reconfigurable atom arrays, d = 3 -> 7); and a Google Willow d=7 chip.
Flag these as secondary citations in the report; I could not verify them from archive text.

**Where the remaining logical error comes from (decoder gap)**
- The gap is not the matching *algorithm* per se, it is that matching decoders are
**factorized into independent X- and Z-graph matchings**, so they structurally cannot use
cross-basis correlations created by Y errors.
- Under SI1000 at p=1.5e-3, R=120: MWPM 2.21e-3 / 6.20e-4 / 1.71e-4 (d=3/5/7) per cycle;
SMD single 1.43e-3 / 3.14e-4 / 1.70e-4 (0.65x, 0.51x, 0.99x); SMD 3-checkpoint ensemble
1.44e-4 at d=7 (0.84x). Belief Matching is the strongest classical baseline at d=7
(7.45e-5, 0.44x). A Libra-style 7-member perturbed-MWPM ensemble gives **<0.5%** improvement

- evidence that the matching family is saturated and the residual error is genuinely
correlated-error information.
- Under depolarizing + perfect stabilizers, joint (lambda_Z, lambda_X) prediction beats the
factorized decoders by 40-91% at d=5-11, growing with d and falling p.
- Round dependence: at short rounds (R=10-25) and low p, k ~ 7 defects and SMD is *worse*
than MWPM (ratio 7.93 at R=10, d=5) - too little signal. It wins from R >= 50 (0.52).
At d=7 it degrades out of distribution at R=140 (1.40). So sparse/neural decoding is not
uniformly better; it needs enough defects to learn from.

**Latency - the real-time constraint (1 us/cycle)**
- Superconducting cycle time ~1 us (2605.17156 Sec. 1). Ideal decoder must be accurate, fast,
and scalable *simultaneously*; the paper frames this as the open problem.
- MWPM: 9.3 / 27.7 / 54.1 us per shot (d=3/5/7) on one CPU core. Belief Matching 19-297 ms.
Tesseract 8-300 ms. SMD batched 83 / 307 / 641 us on an H200.
- Speedups 95-467x over Tesseract, 232-463x over Belief Matching, growing with d.
- Under uniform circuit-level noise, latency grows only 2.4x from d=3 to d=9 (24 -> 57 us,
RTX 4090) vs **773x** for Belief Matching (17 us -> 13.1 ms).

- Honest caveat the authors state themselves: at batch size 1, SMD needs 4-12 ms per shot,
dominated by **GPU kernel-launch overhead, not compute**. It is therefore *not* real-time; a
streaming architecture would be needed. Only AlphaQubit 2-RT on Trillium TPUs reaches <1 us
per cycle to d=11. This is the strongest evidence that the remaining barrier is
**decoder engineering on the hardware interface**, not the code.

**Complexity table worth quoting** (2605.17156 Table 3): MWPM O(n log n) CPU; Tesseract
O(n*B) CPU; AlphaQubit 1 O(d^4 R) on TPU v5e; AlphaQubit 2 O(d^2 R) on Trillium;
dense Mamba O(d^2 R) on RTX 4090; SMD O(k) on RTX 4090 / H200, 7.5-16M params.
Sparsity argument: at p = 1e-3, only ~3% of syndrome entries fire (measured 2.8-3.2% density,
d=3-7), so dense decoding is like a matmul on a 97%-sparse matrix. k/(d^2 R) is roughly
constant across d, so O(k) grows much more slowly than O(d^2 R).

**Main challenges named across the papers**
1. **Correlated / non-factorized errors** - the dominant residual error; needs joint or
learned decoding (above).
2. **Asymmetric error budget** - readout (5p) and idle (4.2p) exceed the entangling gate rate;
this is what pushes the realistic threshold from ~1% down to ~0.5%.
3. **Decoder latency vs the 1 us cycle** - unresolved on commodity hardware; neural decoders
trade accuracy for throughput and vice versa.
4. **Data efficiency / training cost** - SMD needed 1.7-17x *less* training data than the Lange

et al. GNN baseline, yet Sycamore d=5 finetuning used only 480k samples from a single patch
(vs 2.4M for the four d=3 patches); heavy ensembling (16 models at d=5) was needed to pass
dense Mamba there. Experimental-data scarcity is a real constraint.
5. **Leakage and crosstalk** - *not* modelled in any of the papers I read. SI1000 captures
asymmetric Pauli-like rates but not leakage, crosstalk, coherent ZZ, or cosmic-ray-style
correlated bursts. This is a genuine gap in the archive's evidence base and worth stating
plainly in the review: the benchmark thresholds are thresholds *for the noise models that
were simulated*, and the un-modelled physics is exactly the stuff that erodes margin.

1. **Theoretical FT threshold for surface codes:** ~0.5-1% circuit-level for matching decoders;

# Shift 22 Report - res_1 - Paper 1311.2485 "Continuous-time quantum error correction" (Oreshkov, 2013)

File: archive/quantum_error_correction/papers/1311.2485.txt (book chapter, Lidar & Brun eds.; line numbers below refer to this file).
Topic question: *Are surface codes with superconducting qubits capable of operating below fault-tolerant error thresholds?*

- Standard discrete QEC represents noise and correction as discrete CPTP maps with correction applied
after the noise; this is only an approximation, because a real correcting operation takes finite time and
under non-Markovian dynamics the effective map between corrections need not be CP at all (L42-49).
- **CTQEC**: noise *and* correction are continuous. Protected information sits in a subsystem HA of
HS = HA ⊗ HB ⊕ K; in the encoded basis for an [[n,1,r,d]] code, HS = HA ⊗(n-r-1 syndrome qubits)⊗(r gauge qubits)
(L15, L195-206). Multi-qubit QEC then reduces to protecting a *known* single-qubit state.
- **PZ quantum-jump / direct feedback**: ρ -> (1-κdt)ρ + κdt R(ρ), master equation
dρ/dt = L(ρ) + κJ(ρ), J(ρ) = R(ρ) - ρ (L60-73). Physical reading: coupling to a **stream of fresh

ancillas** that continuously pump out accumulated entropy, i.e. a cooling process; also implementable by
weak measurement + weak unitary (L103-108).
- **Weak map form**: ρ -> (1-ε²)ρ + ε²R(ρ) acting over a small but finite time τc, with effective
rate **κ = ε²/τc** (L96-101).
- **ADL indirect feedback**: stochastic master equation with continuous weak measurement of the stabilizer
generators Ml (Wiener-process jumps) plus correcting Hamiltonians Hr switched on with strength
λr(ρ) = λ sgn Tr([Πc, Hr]ρ), chosen to maximize instantaneous code-space fidelity (L128-154).
Weak X-measurement can be done with one ancilla: HX = -X ⊗ Y for time ~ε/2, then destructive ancilla
measurement, outcome probabilities p± = ½(1 ± ε Tr(Xρ)) (L584-600).
## 2. The "freezing" / Zeno argument

- Correctable error weight in a short step Δt is ∝ Δt, uncorrectable (higher-order) weight is O(Δt²);
therefore continuously applied correction stops accumulation, and in the limit Δt -> 0 the state
**freezes** (L112-119).
- Encoded-basis bound: ||dρA/dt|| ≤ B(1-α) + C√(α(1-α)), so keeping (1-α) small suppresses the
accumulation rate of uncorrectable errors; CTQEC is thus "the goal of keeping every syndrome qubit close
to |0>" (L340-364).
## 3. Weak measurement + feedback, and the honest limitation (quoted)

- "All these schemes are to a large extent **heuristic**, and their workings are not thoroughly
understood. The difficulty in rigorously motivating the construction of error-correction protocols based
on weak measurements and feedback is that stochastic evolutions are generally too complicated to study
analytically." (L155-162)
- Both schemes are related to known optimal single-qubit purification protocols: PZ ≈ fast average-fidelity
protocol (measure X, rotate about Y), ADL ≈ fastest-average-time protocol (measure Z, rotate about X);
optimality is claimed only w.r.t. these single-qubit criteria, not for their resource cost (L888-908).
- Retaining the measurement record would improve PZ only by O((1-α*_M)²) - i.e. PZ is "very close to

optimal" in the regime where 1-α*_M is small, but only if the relation between measurement strength and
correcting rotation (Eq. 36, L470-476) can be met (L910-925).
## 4. Numbers and performance (direct feedback, exactly solvable bit-flip models)

- Zeno bookkeeping: α(t) = 1 - Ct² + O(t³) (L1091), and balancing 2√C√(1-α)Δt against
κ(1-α)Δt gives 1 - α*_NM ≈ 4C/κ² vs 1 - α*_M ∝ 1/κ (L1414-1449); same 1/κ² conclusion argued
for general codes because each syndrome qubit in the encoded basis is Zeno-driven (L1450-1454).
- **Resource caveat**: ε ∝ g²τc², hence **κ ∝ g²τc** (L1462-1466). Shrinking τc to gain time
resolution lowers κ; the quadratic gain can outweigh the linear loss, giving a "seemingly paradoxical"
better performance at lower κ (L1468-1474). **This is the failure condition the director asked for.**
## 5. Answers to the four questions

**Q: Does continuous-time correction beat discrete-cycle correction, and under what conditions?**
The paper never benchmarks against a discrete-cycle protocol. What it shows is that CTQEC reaches perfect
protection in the limit of infinite correction rate (freezing), whereas a Markovian discrete cycle always
leaves O(1/r) residual uncorrectable weight that then produces logical errors at rate ~6γ/r (L1057-1077).
So the honest statement is: CTQEC's *floor* is lower and it avoids the dead time of a real correcting
operation, but there is no head-to-head comparison. CTQEC's advantage is real only if the weak operation is
genuinely continuous and cheap; the paper's own resource relation κ ∝ g²τc (L1466) says you pay for
faster resolution with lower correction rate.

**Q: Is the Zeno/freezing result a threshold result or something weaker?**
Much weaker, and it is *not* the foundation of the threshold theorem - the author says so explicitly. The
freezing argument is asymptotic and qualitative: correctable O(Δt) vs uncorrectable O(Δt²) (L112-119).
It has no code-size scaling, no logical error rate per cycle, no threshold constant, and no requirement
that errors be correctable in the discrete sense - it works even below the code's usual error radius
(indeed that is the point). It is also weaker in that it protects *quantum memory*: "So far, CTQEC has been
considered only as a method of protecting quantum memory. ... An important question in this respect is
whether CTQEC can be made fault tolerant" (L1503-1505). Fault tolerance assumes discrete transversal

operations; the author proposes looking for fault-tolerant implementations of a universal set of *weak*
operations, which is an open research programme. Treat the freezing/Zeno result as **an alternative
route to below-threshold behaviour, not a threshold theorem**.

**Q: What would a superconducting surface-code cycle have to look like to realize this?**
The paper contains no surface-code, superconducting, or hardware numbers at all; it is the director's
framing that a ~1 µs surface-code cycle is "coarse, not continuous". Within the paper's own framework
the requirements are explicit and demanding:
(i) τc ≪ the Zeno/bath correlation time, and γδt ≪ 1 ≪ κδt (L1405), i.e. weak, *fast*,
continuously repeated operations at a rate κ well above the noise rate;
(ii) a physically available weak syndrome measurement - the paper's own realization is an ancilla
coupled by HX = -X ⊗ Y, i.e. a two-qubit XX/YY-type interaction plus fast readout (L584-600);

(iii) enough control bandwidth to keep r = κ/λ large *and* linear in n (L1051-1055), since surface
codes have large n and many syndromes;
(iv) locality: the author flags scalability with 1-2 qubit Hamiltonians as an open problem (L1498-1502).
A 1 µs round with measurement/reset latencies of comparable size is in the regime where the
continuous-time description is a poor fit, and where the paper's freezing argument buys nothing beyond
what ordinary threshold analysis already gives.

**Q: What is irrelevant to surface codes, and why should the director not over-claim?**
- No surface code is mentioned anywhere; the only codes analysed are 1- and 3-qubit bit-flip codes
(L1218-1220, L1237-1238). No rotated/unrotated layout, no lattice, no decoder, no threshold value.
- Noise models are independent bit-flips (Markovian) or a single Ising-type bath spin H = γX⊗X
(L70, L1240-1250). No amplitude damping, no leakage, no measurement error, no crosstalk, no cosmic-ray
or quasi-static 1/f drift - the dominant superconducting failure modes. The weakly non-Markovian
bath is modeled as a *single* spin qubit, which is the most favourable possible limit.
- The ADL/feedback family is explicitly labelled heuristic (L155-162); the rigorous analysis exists only

for the quantum-jump (direct feedback) model (L19-23).
- CTQEC is memory protection only; fault tolerance is an open question raised by the author himself
(L1503-1505).
- So the defensible statement is: "continuous-time correction provides a Zeno/freezing mechanism and,
in non-Markovian noise, a 1/κ² rather than 1/κ residual-error law, which is a *complementary* argument
for suppressing logical errors; it is not evidence about surface codes or superconducting thresholds."
Any phrasing like "CTQEC shows surface codes can operate below threshold" would be an extrapolation the
paper does not support.

## Bottom line for the synthesis
Use 1311.2485 for definitional and conceptual framing only: it defines continuous-time correction, gives the
freezing mechanism, the Markovian 1/κ vs non-Markovian 1/κ² contrast, and the honest statement that
continuous-time protection is not yet fault tolerant. Let res_2/res_3/res_4 carry the surface-code and
superconducting evidence.

picture) and ADL indirect feedback (continuous weak stabilizer measurement + fidelity-maximizing
feedback, κ = ε²/τc).
- Freezing: correctable error weight O(Δt), uncorrectable O(Δt²) -> uncorrectable weight does not

accumulate as correction becomes continuous.
- 3-qubit bit-flip, Markovian, r=κ/λ: weight outside code space 3/(4+r) ~ 1/r; residual decay inside
code space like bare bit-flip at rate 6γ/r.
- Cost scales ~linearly in number of qubits for fixed κ.
- Headline: non-Markovian Zeno regime gives quasi-stationary 1-α* ≈ 4C/κ² (quadratic) vs ∝1/κ
(linear) for Markovian. Valid only if γδt << 1 << κδt, i.e. weak correction must resolve the Zeno
time; κ ∝ g²τc so higher time resolution costs correction rate (possible "paradox" of better
performance at lower κ).

- Error *prevention* (measurement only) works only in the Zeno regime, fails for Markovian, needs less
redundancy (4-qubit encoding).

### Bearing on the review question (surface codes + superconducting qubits below threshold)
- CTQEC is an alternative to discrete syndrome cycles, not a threshold result; the paper gives no
surface-code numbers, no threshold values, no rotated/unrotated comparison. Codes studied are 1- and
3-qubit bit-flip.
- Superconducting relevance is a qualitative argument: long T1/T2 and quasi-static 1/f noise mean the
bath memory is non-negligible, i.e. the Zeno/non-Markovian regime where the κ² law applies.
- Author's own open question: can CTQEC be made fault tolerant (FT assumes discrete transversal
ops)? Also open: local-Hamiltonian scalability, equilibrium fidelity for indirect feedback.

- Caution for synthesis: do not let the director claim CTQEC "proves" below-threshold surface-code
operation; it is a 2013 theory chapter with heuristic feedback schemes (author's words).

23:Abstract
24:We propose quaternion-based strategies for quantum error correction by extending quantum mechanics into
25:quaternionic Hilbert spaces. Building on the properties of quaternionic quantum states, we define quaternionic
26:analogues of Pauli operators and quantum gates, ensuring inner product preservation and Hilbert space condi-
27:tions. A simple encoding scheme maps logical qubits into quaternionic systems, introducing natural redundancy
28:and enhanced resilience against noise. We construct a quaternionic extension of the five-qubit code, introducing
29:a framework of 15 syndrome measurements to detect quaternionic errors, including quaternionically rotated error

30:components. Numerical estimates show that the quaternionic five-qubit code achieves a logical error threshold
31:of approximately pth ≈0.015, demonstrating improved performance compared to the standard complex-valued
32:code. These results suggest a new pathway for quantum error correction in high-noise environments, leveraging
33:the richer structure of quaternionic quantum mechanics to improve fault tolerance.

35:Introduction
36:Quantum error correction (QEC) is essential for realizing fault-tolerant quantum computing, protecting fragile
37:quantum states from errors such as bit flips, phase flips, and amplitude damping [1, 2]. Logical qubits are typically

38:formed by entangling multiple physical qubits using codes such as the surface code [3] being a widely studied
39:example. Recent advances include the use of reconfigurable atom arrays to build logical quantum processors [4],
40:where neutral atoms serve as physical qubits. This work demonstrated scalable improvements by increasing the
41:surface code distance from d = 3 to d = 7. Similarly, for superconducting processor achieved below-threshold
42:error correction, showing a logical error suppression factor of λ = 2.14 ± 0.02 by increasing the code distance [5].
43:These developments represent key steps toward scalable quantum computation.
44:Quaternion quantum mechanics (QQM) extends standard quantum mechanics by using quaternions instead
45:of complex numbers. Yang [6] showed that, in a generalized quantum framework, pure states can be uniquely

46:represented as rays in a vector space. This requires the Hilbert space H to be defined in one of the three number
47:fields [7]:
48:• R: real numbers
49:1
50:arXiv:2504.19833v1 [quant-ph] 28 Apr 2025
51:
52:• C: complex numbers
53:• H: quaternions

54:Quaternions were introduced as a natural extension of complex numbers into four dimensions. Quaternions,
55:introduced by Hamilton [8], extend complex numbers to four dimensions and are defined asq = w + xi + yj + zk,
56:where imaginary units satisfy the relations: i2 = j2 = k2 = ijk = −1, to represent quantum states and
57:operators [9]. Here q ∈H, w, x, y, z ∈R and xi + yj + zk is a vector.
58:Adler [10] developed a complete formulation of quantum mechanics in quaternionic Hilbert spaces, aiming
59:for a possible unification with gravity. Later, Danielewski and Sapa [7] derived QQM from a Cauchy elastic
60:continuum model, proposing it as a physically motivated alternative. Their work introduces quaternionic versions
61:of non-relativistic and relativistic wave equations, but does not address QEC. Although QQM is theoretically

62:well established, its application to QEC remains largely unexplored. Existing research on surface codes and color
63:codes [3], and on continuous-variable systems [11], does not consider quaternionic frameworks. In principle, QEC
64:methods such as logical encoding and syndrome measurement can be extended to quaternionic Hilbert spaces,
65:which satisfy the same core postulates as complex ones. However, Vlasov [12] showed that certain QEC schemes
66:fail in standard complex quantum mechanics but succeed in real and quaternionic cases. Adler also suggested
67:the feasibility of quaternionic quantum field theories [13]. Whether quaternions can offer practical advantages
68:for QEC, such as improved error detection or fault tolerance, remains an open question.
69:In this work, we investigate the mathematical foundations and applications of quaternionic quantum mechan-

70:ics (QQM) for quantum error correction. By leveraging the richer algebraic structure of quaternions, we define
71:quaternionic analogues of quantum gates and Pauli operators, and construct new error correction schemes. In par-
72:ticular, we extend the five-qubit code into a quaternionic Hilbert space, introducing 15 syndrome measurements
73:to detect quaternionic errors. We also compare the logical error performance of the standard and quaternionic
74:codes, showing improved resilience against noise and decoherence. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2
75:introduces the mathematical foundations of QQM, emphasizing quaternion algebra in error detection. Section 3
76:presents quaternionic Pauli-like operators, error classification, and syndrome mapping. Section 4 compares the
77:logical error rates of the standard and quaternion-extended five-qubit codes. Section 5 concludes with a summary

78:and future directions.

3
Method: Sparse Mamba Decoder
A physical Pauli error on a data qubit persists until corrected; left in place, it would cause its
adjacent stabilizers to fire every subsequent round, producing a dense “always-on” syndrome. The
detection event di,t = si,t ⊕si,t−1 converts this persistent state into a sparse spacetime signal:
each error contributes detection events only at the endpoints of its trajectory in spacetime,
where it appears and where it is cancelled. This is the structural reason the syndrome volume is

overwhelmingly zero at physical error rates of interest.
For a distance-d surface code with R rounds of stabilizer measurements, the syndrome volume
contains (d2 −1) × R entries, but the expected number of active detection events is
E[k] ≈(d2 −1) × R × ρ(p),

## Topic: Retrieval vs Long Context for Question Answering with LLMs

1. **2310.03025: "Retrieval meets Long Context Large Language Models"** (ICLR 2024, NVIDIA)
- Compared retrieval-augmentation vs long context window using GPT-43B and Llama2-70B on 9 long-context tasks
- Key findings:
- 4K context LLM + retrieval ≈ 16K context LLM (avg score 29.32 vs 29.45 for GPT-43B; 36.02 vs 36.78 for Llama2-70B)
- Retrieval improves BOTH short (4K) AND long (16K/32K) context LLMs
- Best model: retrieval-augmented Llama2-70B-32k (avg 43.6) outperforms GPT-3.5-turbo-16k (42.8) and Davinci-003
- Retrieval-augmented 32K model is ~4x faster on NarrativeQA
- Top-5 retrieved chunks optimal; more chunks (top-10, top-20) can hurt performance (lost-in-the-middle)
- Contradicts LongBench (Bai et al. 2023) which found retrieval only helps small models - this paper attributes difference to model size (70B vs 6B/7B)

2. **2404.15574: "Retrieval Head Mechanistically Explains Long-Context Factuality"** (arXiv 2024)
- Mechanistic interpretability study across 4 model families, 6 scales, 3 finetuning types
- Discovered "retrieval heads" - special attention heads that perform conditional copy-paste from input to output
- Properties of retrieval heads:
- Universal: all long-context capable models have them
- Sparse: <5% of attention heads are retrieval heads
- Intrinsic: exist in base models pretrained with short context; same heads used after context extension
- Dynamically activated: strongest heads always active; weaker heads context-dependent

- Causal: pruning retrieval heads → hallucination; pruning random heads → no effect
- Retrieval heads critical for:
- Needle-in-a-Haystack (factuality)
- Extractive QA (document QA)
- Chain-of-thought reasoning (model needs to refer back to context)
- NOT critical for: tasks using internal knowledge (no CoT)

3. **Wikipedia: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)**
- Overview of RAG technique, process, applications, improvements, challenges
- Key points: RAG reduces hallucinations but doesn't eliminate them; enables domain-specific/updated info; reduces retraining needs; allows source citation

### Key Synthesis Points:
- Retrieval and long context are COMPLEMENTARY, not competing approaches
- Retrieval heads provide mechanistic explanation for WHY retrieval works with long context
- Larger models (70B) benefit more from retrieval than smaller models (7B)
- Optimal retrieval: top-5 chunks; more chunks can hurt due to lost-in-the-middle
- Retrieval heads are intrinsic to pretraining - context extension doesn't create new ones, just activates existing ones

## Topic: Mixture of Experts - Sparse MoE vs Dense Models

1. **2503.03213: "Convergence Rates for Softmax Gating Mixture of Experts"** (arXiv 2025, Nguyen, Ho, Rinaldo)
- Theoretical analysis of MoE convergence rates under softmax gating, dense-to-sparse gating, and hierarchical MoE
- Key findings:
- **Strong identifiability condition**: Expert functions must have linearly independent derivatives (satisfied by 2-layer FFNs with GELU/sigmoid/tanh; violated by linear experts)
- **Convergence rates**:
- Strongly identifiable experts (FFNs): Polynomial rates Oₚ([log(n)/n]¹ᐟ²) exactly-specified, Oₚ([log(n)/n]¹ᐟ⁴) over-specified
- Linear experts: Slower than any polynomial Oₚ(1/log^λ(n)) - requires exponential data O(exp(ε⁻¹ᐟˡ))
- **Parameter interaction**: Linear experts create PDE coupling gating params ω and expert params (a,b): ∂²F/∂ω∂b = ∂F/∂a

- **Dense-to-sparse gating**: Linear router induces temperature-gating interaction slowing convergence even for FFN experts; fix = algebraically independent router (MLP + non-linearity)
- **HMoE**: Same pattern - strongly identifiable experts → polynomial rates; linear experts → exponential rates with cross-level contamination
- **Practical implications**: (i) Use FFN experts (standard in Transformers), not linear; (ii) For dense-to-sparse gating, use non-linear router

### Key Synthesis Points:
- **Theoretical foundation for compute efficiency**: Polynomial convergence rates justify that sparse MoE with proper architecture (FFN experts, softmax gating) can match dense models at matched training compute
- **Architecture is critical**: The standard Transformer MoE design (FFN experts + softmax gating) falls exactly in the "strongly identifiable" regime with fast polynomial rates
- **Explains empirical success**: Mixtral, DeepSeekMoE etc. work because they use architectures that satisfy the strong identifiability condition
- **Connects to res_1's paper (2402.14800)**: Theory explains why expert pruning/skipping works - experts are statistically identifiable and learnable, so some can be pruned without catastrophic loss

Introduction
Quantum error-correcting codes (QECCs) have turned out to have many applications; but their
primary purpose, of course, is to protect quantum information from noise. This need manifests
itself in two rather different situations. The ﬁrst is in quantum computing. The bits in a quantum
computer are subject to noise due both to imprecision in the operations (or gates) and to interac-
tions with the external environment. They undergo errors when they are acted upon, and when
they are just being stored (though hopefully not at the same rate). All the qubits in the computer

must be kept error-free long enough for the computation to be completed. This is the principle of
fault-tolerance.
A rather different situation occurs in quantum communication. Here, the sender and receiver
(Alice and Bob) are assumed to be physically separated, and the qubits travel from the sender
to the receiver over a (presumably noisy) channel. This channel is assumed to be the dominant
source of errors. While the qubits may undergo processing before and after transmission, errors
during this processing are considered negligible compared to the channel errors. This picture of
transmission through a channel is very close to the picture underlying classical information theory.

The types of codes that are of interest in quantum computation and quantum communication
may be quite different. In computation, reliability is key. Therefore, codes with a high distance
(such as concatenated codes) are used. Also, the choice of code may be highly constrained in
other ways: for instance, it is very important that the codes allow efﬁcient circuits for encoded
logic gates (such as the transversal gates allowed by the Steane code). The more efﬁcient these
circuits, the better the fault-tolerant threshold. (See [LB13, chapter 5] for a fuller discussion of
this.)
By contrast, in communication one often imagines sending a very large number of quantum

bits, perhaps even a continuous stream of qubits (as in the convolutional codes of [LB13, chapter
9]). Here, one is generally trying to maximize the rate of transmission, often by encoding many
qubits into a large block, within the constraint of a low error probability for the block. In the
asymptotic limit, one would like to achieve the actual capacity of the channel—the maximum rate
of communication possible.
Because the sender and receiver are separated, joint unitary transformations are impossible.
However, they might be able to draw on other resources, such as extra classical communication,
pre-shared randomness, or pre-shared entanglement. In this chapter we study the use of pre-

shared entanglement in quantum communication, and how we can design QECCs that use entan-
glement to boost either the rate of communication or the number of errors that can be corrected.
Codes that use pre-shared entanglement are called entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting
codes (EAQECCs). We will study a large class of these codes that generalizes the usual stabilizer
formalism from [LB13, chapter 2]. We will also see how these codes can readily be constructed
from classical linear codes, and how they can be useful tools in building standard QECCs.
1.1
Entanglement-assisted codes

In a standard QECC, the encoding operation proceeds in two steps. First, to the quantum state |ψ⟩
of k qubits that one wishes to encode, one appends some number of ancilla qubits in a standard
state (usually |0⟩), and then applies an encoding unitary Uenc:
|ψ⟩→|ψ⟩⊗|0⟩⊗n−k →|ΨL⟩= Uenc|ψ⟩⊗|0⟩⊗n−k,
(1)
where |ΨL⟩is the encoded or logical state. The systems in states |ψ⟩and |0⟩are initially in the
possession of Alice, the sender. The encoding unitary acts on the space of the input qubits and
1

ancillas together.
In an EAQECC, one can append not only ancillas, but also ebits, before doing the encoding
unitary:
|ψ⟩→|ψ⟩⊗|0⟩⊗n−k−c ⊗|Φ+⟩⊗c

The states |Φ+⟩AB are EPR pairs shared between the sender (Alice) and the receiver (Bob). The

encoding operation Uenc acts on the qubits in Alice’s possession; we write (Uenc ⊗ˆIB) above to
indicate that the encoding acts as the identity on Bob’s halves of the ebits. Obviously, in order to
append c ebits to the information qubits, Alice and Bob must have c ebits of pre-shared entangle-
ment. After Alice does the encoding, all of her qubits are sent through the channel, including the
c halves of ebits. So this procedure consumes c ebits of preshared entanglement.
Figure 1: Schematic structure of an entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting code. Alice
and Bob share ebits that Alice uses in encoding her quantum information; these qubits all pass
through the noisy channel, but Bob’s halves of the initial ebits do not.

However, note that Bob’s halves of the c ebits do not pass through the channel. These ebits
were prepared ahead of time, by entanglement distillation or a similar procedure (see [BBP+96,
BDSW96] and [LB13, chapter 22]). Because Bob’s qubits do not pass through the channel, they are
assumed to be error-free.
Why should we wish to use shared entanglement in our encoding? There are two ways to see
how this could enhance the power of the code. First, we can compare EAQECCs to teleportation. In
teleportation, an ebit can be used (in combination with classical communication) to transmit one
qubit perfectly from the sender to the receiver. We might therefore expect that making use of ebits

in error-correction could boost the rate of transmission.
Second, we can compare EAQECCs to superdense coding. In superdense coding, by using an
ebit the sender can send two classical bits of information to the receiver by means of a single
qubit. Each ancilla bit in a standard QECC can be thought of as holding one classical bit of infor-
mation about any errors that have occurred. Replacing an ancilla with one half of an ebit could,
in principle, allow the receiver to extract two bits of classical information about the errors; with
more information, more errors can be corrected. We shall see, in the constructions that follow,
that we can think of the enhanced power of EAQECCs in both of these ways, but the superdense

coding interpretation is more often the best ﬁt. EAQECCs can achieve some communication tasks
with fewer resources (or less chance of error) than would be needed by a standard QECC plus
teleportation [HW10b].
The possibility of constructing entanglement-assisted codes was suggested in [BDSW96], though
no practical codes were constructed. From asymptotic results in quantum information theory, we
know that having pre-shared entanglement allows an enhanced rate of quantum communication
2

between a sender and receiver [DHW04, DHW08]. EAQECCs are the ﬁnite-length realization
of this idea. By constructing larger and larger code blocks, in principle one can approach the
entanglement-assisted quantum capacity of the channel. An example of such a code was con-
structed by Bowen in [Bow02], starting from a standard stabilizer QECC (see [LB13, chapter 2]). In
[BDH06, BDH14, HDB07] an essentially complete theory of stabilizer EAQECCs was constructed.
That is the theory presented in this chapter.
Note, however, that in general shared entanglement does not come for free: entanglement
must be established between the sender and receiver, and this in general requires the use of quan-

tum channels, and perhaps additional entanglement puriﬁcation. Therefore, EAQECCs do not
outperform standard quantum codes under all circumstances. The enhanced communication rates
that come from the use of entanglement must be paid for in establishing the entanglement in the
ﬁrst place. For many purposes, what is important is the net rate of the code: the number of qubits
transmitted minus the number of ebits consumed. With this measure, EAQECCs tend to perform
about the same as standard codes. Even in this case, though, EAQECCs sometimes have advan-
tages: as we shall see, there are many fewer restrictions on the construction of EAQECCs than
standard codes.

2.1
Noncommuting “stabilizers”
First, let us recall the stabilizer formalism for conventional quantum error-correcting codes, as
presented in [LB13, chapter 2]. Let Gn be the n-qubit Pauli group [NC00]. Every operator in

2.6

General codes and code parameters
The canonical code described above is not very useful for actual error correction. It corrects a
set of highly nonlocal errors, of a type that are not likely to occur in reality. However, it is very
helpful in clarifying how the process of error correction works, and the role of the resources used
in encoding. Each added ancilla can contain, in principle, one bit of information about any errors
that occur. Each shared ebit between the sender and receiver can contain two bits of information
about errors. This information about the errors is retrieved by measuring the stabilizer generators.
After Alice’s qubits have passed through the channel, Bob has all the qubits and can perform these

measurements.
A general EAQECC has exactly the same algebraic structure as the canonical code. The en-
coded state, before going through the channel, has c ebits of entanglement with the c qubits on
12

Bob’s side. Corresponding to this entanglement are c pairs of stabilizer generators. Each pair
of generators has the following structure: a pair of anticommuting operators on Alice’s qubits,
tensored with a Z and an X, respectively, on one of the qubits on Bob’s side to “resolve” the anti-
commutativity. These pairs of generators are the symplectic pairs of the EAQECC. In addition to
these pairs, there can be single generators that act as the identity on all of Bob’s qubits. These are
the isotropic generators. For an [[n, k, d; c]] EAQECC, each of the stabilizer elements acts on n + c
qubits, n on Alice’s side and c on Bob’s side; there is a set of n −k generators for the stabilizer
chosen in a standard form, with 2c symplectic pairs of generators and s = n −k −2c isotropic

generators.
By Lemma 2, if two sets of Pauli operators can be put in one-to-one correspondence so that
they have the same commutation relations, there is a unitary transformation that turns one set
into the other (up to a phase). The n −k generators of an [[n, k; c]] EAQECC can be mapped by a
unitary operator UE to the generators of a canonical code.
It is important to realize is that the canonical code describes the input of the EAQECC before
encoding. It describes a set of k information qubits, c ebits, and s ancillas. The unitary UE trans-
forms the stabilizer for this input into the stabilizer for the EAQECC. Therefore UE is a unitary

encoding operator for this code. It transforms the localized states of the input qubits into nonlo-
cal, entangled states spread over all the qubits. By this transformation, the correctable error set is
transformed from the strange, nonlocal errors of the canonical code to a more physically realistic
set of errors (most commonly, localized errors on the individual qubits).

Title: New Approach to Quantum Error Correction
arXiv ID: 1401.0456

New Approach to Quantum Error Correction
Ri Qu, Bing-jian Shang, Yan-ru Bao and Yi-ping Ma
School of Computer Science and Technology, Tianjin University, Tianjin, 300072, China and
Tianjin Key Laboratory of Cognitive Computing and Application, Tianjin, 300072, China

Operator quantum error correction provides a unified framework for the known techniques of
quantum error correction such as the standard error correction model, the method of
decoherence-free subspaces, and the noiseless subsystem method. We first show an example of a
new quantum error correction scheme which can not be described by operation quantum error
correction. Then we introduce a different notion of noiseless subsystems according to the example.
Base on this notion, we present a more unified approach which incorporates operator quantum
error correction as a special case. Moreover, we also give a sufficient and necessary condition of
quantum error correction using this approach. We show that this approach provides more recovery

operations than operator quantum error correction, which possibly leads to simpler decoding
procedures.

ampliate noiseless subsystems, we introduce a more unified approach to quantum error correction,
so-called GOQEC. We obtain an important consequence: the existence of OQEC codes is
equivalent to one of GOQEC codes. While GOQEC model does not lead to new families of codes,
it does allow for new error correction procedures, possibly enriching the fault tolerance quantum
computing theory. For example, it is possible for some experiments of QEC that GOQEC codes
are easier to detect and recover errors than OQEC ones because the former provides more
recovery operations than the latter. This implies that we might construct simpler fault-tolerant
gates by means of GOQEC.

4
Catalytic QECCs
EAQECCs make use of an additional resource—prior shared entanglement—to boost the power of
an error-correcting code. This paradigm raises several theoretical and practical questions, which

address how these codes might be useful in practice, and how they ﬁt into different families of
codes that draw on different resources.
The ﬁrst practical question is: how was this entanglement shared in the ﬁrst place? If the
sender and receiver communicate by a noisy quantum channel, then the entanglement would
have to be shared through this channel. Alice locally prepares EPR pairs, and sends half of each
pair through the channel, either protected by a standard QECC, or making use of entanglement
puriﬁcation techniques [BBP+96, BDSW96] to produce a smaller number of perfect EPR pairs.
So we see that in this context the enhanced rate of an EAQECC must be paid for by additional

channel communication to establish the entanglement in the ﬁrst place. This means that for many
purposes it is the net rate (k −c)/n of the EAQECC that is the appropriate ﬁgure of merit. This net
rate need not be better than that achieved by a standard QECC; indeed, it is quite possible for the
net rate to be zero or negative.
Even a code with a negative net rate may actually be useful in practice. One great advantage of
shared entanglement as a resource is that it is independent of the message being sent, and can in
principle be prepared well ahead of time. One natural application of EAQECCs would therefore
be to a quantum network where usage varies at different times. During periods of low usage,

shared entanglement could be built up between the sender and receiver. During periods of high
usage, this shared entanglement could be drawn on to increase the rate of transmission without
sacriﬁcing error-correcting power.
EAQECCs with positive net rates can be used in other ways to improve the power and ﬂexi-
bility of quantum communications. To illustrate this, let us consider the idea of a catalytic code.
Here, in addition to n uses of a noisy channel, the sender may send c qubits noise-free. One obvi-
ous approach is to send c information qubits using the noise-free bits, and then send k more qubits
through the channel by means of an [[n, k]] standard QECC. However, another way of proceeding

would be to use the c noise-free bits to establish c ebits between Alice and Bob, and then use an
[[n, k′; c]] EAQECC. So long as k′ ≥k + c (and both codes are assumed to correct the errors in the
channel), one does as well or better with the second approach as with the straightforward one. In
this case, the noise-free qubits are used to boost the rate of the noisy qubits. We call a procedure
of this type a catalytic code—the c noise-free qubits enhance transmission by an amount equal to at
least c.
In practice, noise-free transmission is not really possible. However, it is possible to simulate
it by using a standard QECC to protect the c noise-free qubits. Suppose that we start with an

[[n, k; c]] EAQECC. To establish c ebits with Bob, Alice would need to send c qubits through the
channel. Suppose that she protects them with an [[n′, c]] standard QECC. Then we can think of the
full block of n + n′ qubits that go through the channel as a single codeword; by putting these two
codes together we have constructed an [[n + n′, k]] standard QECC.
Of course, the second code could also be an EAQECC. If we have an [[n, k; c]] EAQECC and an
[[n′, k′; c′]] EAQECC, we can send Bob’s halves of the c ebits in the second code block, so long as
16

k′ ≥c. By putting these two code blocks together, we have constructed an [[n + n′, k + k′ −c; c′]]
EAQECC.
Nor need we combine only two codes in this way. One rather simple construction is as follows:
take an [[n, k; c]] EAQECC with positive net rate, and encode Bob’s halves of the c ebits in another
copy of the same code. Repeat this M times, and one quickly builds up a much larger block code:
an [[Mn, M(k −c) + c; c]] EAQECC. This procedure is called bootstrapping. Two observations of
this new code are quickly evident: ﬁrst, as M becomes large, the rate of the code approaches the
net rate (k −c)/n of the original code. Second, as M becomes large, the rate of entanglement usage

c/Mn becomes small. By bootstrapping we have built a large code whose rate is the net rate of
the original code, and which uses relatively little entanglement.
Practically speaking there is a limit to how big M can be; if the block size becomes too large, the
probability that one of the sub-blocks of n qubits will have an uncorrectable error becomes high,
and the code will no longer be useful. At this point, little is known about the practical performance
of catalytic codes—more research is needed.
By this approach we see another use of EAQECCs: rather than being used themselves directly,
they can be used as building blocks for the construction of standard codes. Because EAQECCs

can be constructed from classical codes without the need to satisfy the dual-containing constraint,
they in some cases will outperform standard codes with otherwise similar parameters. Combin-
ing EAQECCs with each other, or with standard codes, may allow the relatively easy construction
of standard codes with good error-correcting properties. Moreover, this may lead to applica-
tions of EAQECCs beyond the quantum communication paradigm, using them to construct stan-
dard codes that might be useful in other applications (such as quantum computing). However, at
present this is pure speculation: such applications have yet to be studied.
5

Conclusions
EAQECCs expand the usual paradigm of quantum error correction by allowing the sender and
receiver to make use of pre-shared entanglement. This entanglement can increase either the rate
of communication or the number of correctable errors. While entanglement can be used to im-
prove quantum communication in other ways—for example, by sending classical information
through the channel and teleporting extra qubits—in many cases EAQECCs have better perfor-
mance [HW10a, HW10b].
In this chapter we have presented an extension of the usual stabilizer formalism for QECCs

to include entanglement-assistance. This extension includes the usual theory of stabilizers as a
special case, and has a number of advantages; in particular, it allows one to construct quantum
codes from classical linear codes without having to impose the dual-containing constraint of stan-
dard codes, while retaining the usual relation between the rate and distance of the classical and
quantum codes. Moreover, if entanglement-assistance is allowed, one can in some cases outdo the
performance of the best standard QECC by optimizing without the dual-containing constraint.
In quantum communication protocols involving entanglement, the applications of EAQECCs
are obvious. However, the construction may also be useful in other cases, by using EAQECCs as

catalytic codes. In this case, we are essentially using EAQECCs as building blocks for standard
codes, or for codes that use only a small amount of pre-existing entanglement. In these construc-
tions the net rate of the EAQECCs is the most important parameter; this net rate can be directly
calculated from the classical linear code, for codes constructed from classical precursors.
Because these constructions do not require dual-containing codes, it is possible to directly de-
rive quantum versions of highly-efﬁcient modern codes, such as Turbo codes and LDPC codes

# Shift 27 Summary - res_3 - Nested QEC & Operator QEC

## Papers Reviewed
1. **0909.5103**: "Nested Quantum Error Correction Codes" (Wang, Sun, Fan, Vedral, 2009/2021)
2. **1401.0456**: "New Approach to Quantum Error Correction" (Qu, Shang, Bao, Ma, 2014) - GOQEC / ampliate noiseless subsystems
## 1. Nested QEC (0909.5103) - Key Findings

### What the Paper Does
- **Core construction**: A general method to build new QECCs by "nesting" a **blockcode** and a **subcode** together
- **Mechanism**: Blockcode provides syndromes for errors within blocks; subcode provides syndromes to distinguish *which* block had the error
- **Commuting condition**: Eq. (2) - blockcode and subcode generators must commute
- **Claims**: "Works for all length and all distance codes" (line 19); "quite efficient to construct optimal or near optimal codes" (line 20)
- **Unification**: Shows **concatenation** (lines 3997-4000) and **Gottesman's stabilizer pasting** (lines 384-386, 2622-2624, 4002-4109) are special cases of nesting

### Why This Does NOT Help Surface Codes
| Aspect | Nested/Concatenated Codes | Surface Codes |
|--------|---------------------------|---------------|
| **Construction** | Hierarchical: small codes → large codes via nesting/concatenation | Single topological stabilizer code on 2D lattice |
| **Distance scaling** | Distance multiplies (e.g., d₁ × d₂ for concatenation) | Distance = lattice size (grow patch) |
| **Locality** | Non-local generators across blocks | **Strictly local** (weight-4 plaquette/star) |
| **Threshold** | Typically low (~10⁻⁴ - 10⁻⁵) | **High** (~1% for phenomenological noise) |
| **Decoding** | Hierarchical / complex | MWPM / neural / union-find (efficient) |

**Blunt assessment**: The nesting/concatenation lens is a **distraction** for surface codes. The surface code's high threshold comes precisely from being a *local topological code*, not from concatenation. Nesting theory addresses a different problem: how to construct *good parameters* [[n,k,d]] for arbitrary n,d. Surface codes solve this by geometry, not algebra.

### What the Director Must NOT Claim
- ❌ "Nested QEC provides a framework for building better surface codes" — false; surface codes are not built by nesting
- ❌ "Concatenation theory predicts surface code thresholds" — false; concatenated codes have much lower thresholds
- ❌ "This paper gives any error rate or threshold numbers" — it does not
## 2. Operator QEC / GOQEC (1401.0456) - Key Findings

### What the Paper Does
- **Identifies a gap**: Standard OQEC (Kribs-Laflamme-Poulin 2005) uses "normal noiseless subsystems" where noisy subsystem B maps to itself under the channel
- **New notion**: **"Ampliate noiseless subsystems"** (Def. 1, line 1362) - channel can map B to *any* subsystem B' (including dim B' < dim B)
- **GOQEC framework**: Generalized OQEC incorporating ampliate noiseless subsystems
- **Key theorem (Thm 2, lines 2464-2519)**: **GOQEC and OQEC have exactly the same set of correctable codes** (same [[n,k,d]] codes exist)
- **But**: GOQEC provides **more recovery operations** than OQEC (lines 2424-2426, 2724-2726, 3183-3184)

### "Simpler Decoding" Claim - Assessment
**The paper's claim** (lines 17-18, 2724-2727, 3183-3185): "GOQEC provides more recovery operations... which possibly leads to simpler decoding procedures... possibly enriching fault tolerance... might construct simpler fault-tolerant gates"

**My assessment**: **No threshold-relevant meaning established.**
- **No error rates, no thresholds, no hardware data** - purely algebraic
- **"Possibly leads to simpler decoding"** is speculation (lines 18, 2726, 3184 use "possibly", "might")
- **No concrete decoding algorithm** is given, let alone complexity analysis
- **No connection to surface code decoding** (MWPM, union-find, neural decoders)
- **Recovery operation count ≠ decoding complexity**: Decoding = syndrome → correction mapping; recovery = physical implementation of correction. More recovery choices don't automatically simplify the *classical* decoding problem.

### What the Director Must NOT Claim
- ❌ "GOQEC proves simpler decoding for surface codes" — no surface code analysis, no decoding complexity results
- ❌ "Ampliate noiseless subsystems improve fault-tolerant thresholds" — no threshold analysis at all
- ❌ "This paper provides practical decoding algorithms" — it provides algebraic conditions, not algorithms
- ❌ "More recovery operations = lower logical error rate" — unproven; could even increase logical errors if wrong recovery chosen
## 3. Cross-Paper Synthesis: What Helps Surface Codes?

| Paper | Helps Surface Codes? | Why / Why Not |
|-------|---------------------|---------------|
| **Nested QEC (0909.5103)** | **No** | Addresses code *construction* for arbitrary [[n,k,d]]; surface codes use *geometry* not concatenation. Different design philosophy entirely. |
| **GOQEC (1401.0456)** | **No (theoretically possible, practically no)** | Proves same codes exist; offers more recovery maps. But: no decoding algorithms, no threshold analysis, no hardware mapping. "Simpler decoding" is an untested hypothesis. |

### What Actually Determines "Below Threshold" for Surface Codes on Superconducting Qubits
These papers **do not address**:
1. **Physical error rates** (T₁, T₂, gate fidelity, crosstalk, leakage)
2. **Syndrome extraction circuit depth & fidelity**
3. **Decoder performance at realistic error rates** (MWPM, neural, etc.)
4. **Correlated / non-Markovian noise** (both papers assume i.i.d. or simple channels)
5. **Architecture constraints** (planar connectivity, frequency collisions, readout errors)
6. **Logical error rate vs. distance scaling** (the actual threshold signature)

**Nested QEC (0909.5103)**: A code-construction framework unifying concatenation and pasting. **Irrelevant to surface codes** — surface codes achieve high threshold *because* they are local topological codes, not concatenated codes. Do not cite this as theoretical support for surface code thresholds.

**GOQEC (1401.0456)**: A mathematical generalization of OQEC via "ampliate noiseless subsystems." Proves **same codes, more recovery maps**. Claims "possibly simpler decoding" but provides **zero evidence**: no algorithms, no complexity bounds, no threshold analysis, no surface code connection. Do not claim this improves fault-tolerant thresholds or decoding.

**What the director must NOT claim based on these two papers**:
1. That nested/concatenation theory explains or predicts surface code performance
2. That GOQEC/ampliate subsystems yield practical decoding improvements
3. That either paper provides error rates, thresholds, or hardware-relevant predictions
4. That "more recovery operations" translates to "simpler decoding" or "better thresholds"
**What these papers actually are**: Pure code-theoretic / operator-algebraic formalism papers. Useful for classifying what codes *exist*, silent on what codes *work* on superconducting hardware.

# Shift 22 Report - res_1 - Paper 1311.2485 "Continuous-time quantum error correction" (Oreshkov, 2013)

File: archive/quantum_error_correction/papers/1311.2485.txt (book chapter, Lidar & Brun eds.; line numbers below refer to this file).
Topic question: *Are surface codes with superconducting qubits capable of operating below fault-tolerant error thresholds?*

- Standard discrete QEC represents noise and correction as discrete CPTP maps with correction applied
after the noise; this is only an approximation, because a real correcting operation takes finite time and
under non-Markovian dynamics the effective map between corrections need not be CP at all (L42-49).
- **CTQEC**: noise *and* correction are continuous. Protected information sits in a subsystem HA of
HS = HA ⊗ HB ⊕ K; in the encoded basis for an [[n,1,r,d]] code, HS = HA ⊗(n-r-1 syndrome qubits)⊗(r gauge qubits)
(L15, L195-206). Multi-qubit QEC then reduces to protecting a *known* single-qubit state.
- **PZ quantum-jump / direct feedback**: ρ -> (1-κdt)ρ + κdt R(ρ), master equation
dρ/dt = L(ρ) + κJ(ρ), J(ρ) = R(ρ) - ρ (L60-73). Physical reading: coupling to a **stream of fresh

ancillas** that continuously pump out accumulated entropy, i.e. a cooling process; also implementable by
weak measurement + weak unitary (L103-108).
- **Weak map form**: ρ -> (1-ε²)ρ + ε²R(ρ) acting over a small but finite time τc, with effective
rate **κ = ε²/τc** (L96-101).
- **ADL indirect feedback**: stochastic master equation with continuous weak measurement of the stabilizer
generators Ml (Wiener-process jumps) plus correcting Hamiltonians Hr switched on with strength
λr(ρ) = λ sgn Tr([Πc, Hr]ρ), chosen to maximize instantaneous code-space fidelity (L128-154).
Weak X-measurement can be done with one ancilla: HX = -X ⊗ Y for time ~ε/2, then destructive ancilla
measurement, outcome probabilities p± = ½(1 ± ε Tr(Xρ)) (L584-600).
## 2. The "freezing" / Zeno argument

- Correctable error weight in a short step Δt is ∝ Δt, uncorrectable (higher-order) weight is O(Δt²);
therefore continuously applied correction stops accumulation, and in the limit Δt -> 0 the state
**freezes** (L112-119).
- Encoded-basis bound: ||dρA/dt|| ≤ B(1-α) + C√(α(1-α)), so keeping (1-α) small suppresses the
accumulation rate of uncorrectable errors; CTQEC is thus "the goal of keeping every syndrome qubit close
to |0>" (L340-364).
## 3. Weak measurement + feedback, and the honest limitation (quoted)

- "All these schemes are to a large extent **heuristic**, and their workings are not thoroughly
understood. The difficulty in rigorously motivating the construction of error-correction protocols based
on weak measurements and feedback is that stochastic evolutions are generally too complicated to study
analytically." (L155-162)
- Both schemes are related to known optimal single-qubit purification protocols: PZ ≈ fast average-fidelity
protocol (measure X, rotate about Y), ADL ≈ fastest-average-time protocol (measure Z, rotate about X);
optimality is claimed only w.r.t. these single-qubit criteria, not for their resource cost (L888-908).
- Retaining the measurement record would improve PZ only by O((1-α*_M)²) - i.e. PZ is "very close to

optimal" in the regime where 1-α*_M is small, but only if the relation between measurement strength and
correcting rotation (Eq. 36, L470-476) can be met (L910-925).
## 4. Numbers and performance (direct feedback, exactly solvable bit-flip models)

- Zeno bookkeeping: α(t) = 1 - Ct² + O(t³) (L1091), and balancing 2√C√(1-α)Δt against
κ(1-α)Δt gives 1 - α*_NM ≈ 4C/κ² vs 1 - α*_M ∝ 1/κ (L1414-1449); same 1/κ² conclusion argued
for general codes because each syndrome qubit in the encoded basis is Zeno-driven (L1450-1454).
- **Resource caveat**: ε ∝ g²τc², hence **κ ∝ g²τc** (L1462-1466). Shrinking τc to gain time
resolution lowers κ; the quadratic gain can outweigh the linear loss, giving a "seemingly paradoxical"
better performance at lower κ (L1468-1474). **This is the failure condition the director asked for.**
## 5. Answers to the four questions

**Q: Does continuous-time correction beat discrete-cycle correction, and under what conditions?**
The paper never benchmarks against a discrete-cycle protocol. What it shows is that CTQEC reaches perfect
protection in the limit of infinite correction rate (freezing), whereas a Markovian discrete cycle always
leaves O(1/r) residual uncorrectable weight that then produces logical errors at rate ~6γ/r (L1057-1077).
So the honest statement is: CTQEC's *floor* is lower and it avoids the dead time of a real correcting
operation, but there is no head-to-head comparison. CTQEC's advantage is real only if the weak operation is
genuinely continuous and cheap; the paper's own resource relation κ ∝ g²τc (L1466) says you pay for
faster resolution with lower correction rate.

**Q: Is the Zeno/freezing result a threshold result or something weaker?**
Much weaker, and it is *not* the foundation of the threshold theorem - the author says so explicitly. The
freezing argument is asymptotic and qualitative: correctable O(Δt) vs uncorrectable O(Δt²) (L112-119).
It has no code-size scaling, no logical error rate per cycle, no threshold constant, and no requirement
that errors be correctable in the discrete sense - it works even below the code's usual error radius
(indeed that is the point). It is also weaker in that it protects *quantum memory*: "So far, CTQEC has been
considered only as a method of protecting quantum memory. ... An important question in this respect is
whether CTQEC can be made fault tolerant" (L1503-1505). Fault tolerance assumes discrete transversal

operations; the author proposes looking for fault-tolerant implementations of a universal set of *weak*
operations, which is an open research programme. Treat the freezing/Zeno result as **an alternative
route to below-threshold behaviour, not a threshold theorem**.

**Q: What would a superconducting surface-code cycle have to look like to realize this?**
The paper contains no surface-code, superconducting, or hardware numbers at all; it is the director's
framing that a ~1 µs surface-code cycle is "coarse, not continuous". Within the paper's own framework
the requirements are explicit and demanding:
(i) τc ≪ the Zeno/bath correlation time, and γδt ≪ 1 ≪ κδt (L1405), i.e. weak, *fast*,
continuously repeated operations at a rate κ well above the noise rate;
(ii) a physically available weak syndrome measurement - the paper's own realization is an ancilla
coupled by HX = -X ⊗ Y, i.e. a two-qubit XX/YY-type interaction plus fast readout (L584-600);

(iii) enough control bandwidth to keep r = κ/λ large *and* linear in n (L1051-1055), since surface
codes have large n and many syndromes;
(iv) locality: the author flags scalability with 1-2 qubit Hamiltonians as an open problem (L1498-1502).
A 1 µs round with measurement/reset latencies of comparable size is in the regime where the
continuous-time description is a poor fit, and where the paper's freezing argument buys nothing beyond
what ordinary threshold analysis already gives.

**Q: What is irrelevant to surface codes, and why should the director not over-claim?**
- No surface code is mentioned anywhere; the only codes analysed are 1- and 3-qubit bit-flip codes
(L1218-1220, L1237-1238). No rotated/unrotated layout, no lattice, no decoder, no threshold value.
- Noise models are independent bit-flips (Markovian) or a single Ising-type bath spin H = γX⊗X
(L70, L1240-1250). No amplitude damping, no leakage, no measurement error, no crosstalk, no cosmic-ray
or quasi-static 1/f drift - the dominant superconducting failure modes. The weakly non-Markovian
bath is modeled as a *single* spin qubit, which is the most favourable possible limit.
- The ADL/feedback family is explicitly labelled heuristic (L155-162); the rigorous analysis exists only

for the quantum-jump (direct feedback) model (L19-23).
- CTQEC is memory protection only; fault tolerance is an open question raised by the author himself
(L1503-1505).
- So the defensible statement is: "continuous-time correction provides a Zeno/freezing mechanism and,
in non-Markovian noise, a 1/κ² rather than 1/κ residual-error law, which is a *complementary* argument
for suppressing logical errors; it is not evidence about surface codes or superconducting thresholds."
Any phrasing like "CTQEC shows surface codes can operate below threshold" would be an extrapolation the
paper does not support.

## Bottom line for the synthesis
Use 1311.2485 for definitional and conceptual framing only: it defines continuous-time correction, gives the
freezing mechanism, the Markovian 1/κ vs non-Markovian 1/κ² contrast, and the honest statement that
continuous-time protection is not yet fault tolerant. Let res_2/res_3/res_4 carry the surface-code and
superconducting evidence.
